notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 16 below, but two parts of your request are only partly covered. **Section 2 is empty:** I found no Protestant teachers disagreeing along denominational lines on this chapter. **Section 3 is partial:** modern scholarship and Catholic sources are covered, but I found nothing from Orthodox sources or from popular teachers (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace). I also couldn't see the NET Bible's footnotes, because the page loaded without them. The sources I used are Pulpit Commentary, Enduring Word (David Guzik), Gill, Clarke, Constable, Bible Odyssey and the Catholic Encyclopedia.

## 1. The traditional reading

**v. 1:** Pulpit thinks Jehu and his father Hanani both came from Judah. Hanani was jailed for rebuking King Asa, and Jehu later spoke to King Jehoshaphat, so his work as a prophet lasted at least 50 years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik adds that Jehu also wrote history about the kings of Israel (2 Chr 20:34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 2:** For Pulpit, "out of the dust" means Baasha came from humble beginnings, perhaps rising from the ranks. The words don't approve how he took the throne. They only say God used him and overruled even his plotting and cruelty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik says God was at work behind the scenes, even through Baasha's plot against Nadab. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 3:** Pulpit notes that the Hebrew for "consume" means wipe out, the same word used against Jeroboam's house in 14:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik says Baasha wasn't related to Jeroboam by blood, but he was his spiritual heir, so his house got the same sentence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 4:** Pulpit points out that the same words had been spoken against Jeroboam only a few years before, and Baasha knew how they came true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik explains that an unburied body eaten by animals was a special disgrace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 5:** For Pulpit, Baasha's "might" is shown by his fortifying a post about five miles from Jerusalem (15:17–21). Keil, by contrast, read it as energy in governing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 6:** Pulpit's sermon outlines observe that Baasha was as great a criminal as any of his house, yet he came to his grave in peace and honour. He died on his bed and was buried in state. Must there not be future reckoning and retribution? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-16.html

**v. 7:** Pulpit sees this as explaining v. 2, not a second prophecy. It lists other views too: Rawlinson says Baasha was punished partly for killing Jeroboam's family, while Keil and Bähr say the verse stops readers thinking God told him to murder Nadab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik says God used Baasha but didn't make him do it. Baasha already wanted to, so judging him was fair. He quotes Clarke: Scripture often speaks of God "doing" what He only allows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 8:** Guzik notes that Baasha's son reigned only two years, a sign that God did not bless the dynasty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 9:** Pulpit makes several points:
- After Jeroboam, people no longer respected "the Lord's anointed," and grabbing the crown was not seen as sin.
- Zimri only does what Baasha had done.
- Elah should have been with his army, not drinking in a subject's house.
- Arza was very likely in on the plot.
- One older scholar (Stanley) guessed Zimri was a last bid by Saul's family for the throne.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 10:** Pulpit quotes Ewald: three times in Israel, a dynasty's founder was its only strong king, and his son lost the throne after two years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 11:** Pulpit says "kinsman" is the Hebrew *go'el*, the relative whose duty was to avenge a killing. So Zimri was getting rid of anyone who might avenge Elah, and he went further than Baasha by killing the family's friends too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik says this was common in the ancient world, and David's treatment of Saul's family was a rare exception. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 12:** Pulpit's sermon outlines say the threat was carried out in full: God's threatenings are not exaggerations meant to frighten us away from sin; *they are descriptions*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-16.html

**v. 13:** Pulpit says the "worthless idols" here are Jeroboam's golden calves rather than other idols (compare Deut 32:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 15:** Pulpit thinks Baasha probably dropped the siege of Gibbethon and Elah restarted it. Elah stayed away, perhaps because of his self-indulgent habits and the bad memory of Nadab being killed there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 16:** Pulpit says "all Israel" means the army. It turned to Omri because the army's commander stood next to the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik sees here that the people's voice counted for more in Israel than is often thought. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 17:** Pulpit says "marched up" fits the climb from the lowlands to the hill country. The army probably arrived about six or seven days after Elah was killed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 18:** Pulpit explains the "citadel" as the highest, strongest part of the palace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik lists Zimri with the Bible's other suicides. He says Scripture never approves suicide, but it is wrong to treat it as the unforgivable sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 19:** Pulpit says Zimri could do little in seven days, so the verse means his character showed whose side he was on. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik says God may judge sooner rather than later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 20:** Pulpit notes that the writer leaves out his usual "and all that he did," because the plot was all there was to tell about Zimri. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm

**vv. 21–22:** Pulpit admits we can't know who Tibni was. It guesses the army itself was split. Josephus says Omri killed him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik quotes Poole: even civil war did not bring the people to repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/. Constable says Omri finally overpowered Tibni and probably executed him (1 Kings 16:22). One writer argued that Tibni did not necessarily die but simply passed off the scene. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-16.html

**v. 23:** Pulpit points out that the dates don't simply add up to twelve full years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/16.htm. Guzik quotes Clarke's answer: a five-year split with Tibni, then seven years of sole rule. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**v. 24:** Pulpit argues that buying the land permanently broke Leviticus 25:23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-16.html. Guzik says Samaria was a new city with no tribal ties and easy to defend, and digs show Omri was the first to build on the hill. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**vv. 25–26:** Guzik quotes Knapp: Omri seems to have passed laws making idolatry compulsory (Micah 6:16), and these lasted to the end of the kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/. Guzik also notes that outside the Bible Omri was famous. The Moabite Stone calls him Moab's conqueror, and Assyrians called Israel "the house of Omri." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

**vv. 29–30:** Constable says 1 Kings 16:30; 1 Kings 16:33 bracket and set forth Ahab's unusual wickedness with special emphasis. The writer had just written that Omri was the worst king so far. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-16.html

**v. 31:**
- Guzik says Jeroboam worshipped the LORD in a false way, while Ahab brought in new pagan gods altogether. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/
- Guzik notes Jezebel's name was also a Hebrew pun on "dung." He quotes Dilday that a secular historian would have praised the marriage as a smart alliance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/
- Constable says Ahab is rightly blamed for the marriage, since the son could usually refuse an arranged match. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/16-29.html

**vv. 32–33:** GotQuestions (via Precept Austin) says Ahab built a house to Baal in Samaria and made an Asherah pole for pagan worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-16-commentary

**v. 34:**
- **Gill:** Hiel either didn't know Joshua's curse or defied it to please the king and queen. His firstborn died as the foundation was laid, his other children died during the building, and the youngest died at the end. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/16-34.html
- **Constable:** God kept His word about Jericho, and He would keep it about Ahab too. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/16-34.html
- **Guzik:** this was a merciful warning that Ahab ignored. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ
I found no teachers disagreeing along denominational lines on this chapter. The disagreements I did find are between individual commentators: on v. 7 (see Pulpit's list of views) and on v. 34 (below).

## 3. Other views

**v. 24, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says Samaria stayed small, more a royal compound than a multifaceted city. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/samaria/

**vv. 25–26, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says Assyrian records called Israel "house of Omri" long after his dynasty ended, which suggests Israel became a major regional power under him. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-house-of-omri/

**v. 31, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says it is likely Jezebel worshipped Baal. However, Ahab gave his sons names honouring the LORD, so it questions how far she really opposed the LORD's worship. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/jezebel/

**vv. 32–33, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey suggests Ahab may have compromised with Canaanite worship to unite his kingdom, giving Baal equal standing with the LORD. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ahab/. Another of its articles notes an inscription that may mention a temple of the LORD at Samaria, which the Bible doesn't record. https://w.bibleodyssey.org/articles/samaria/

**v. 34, did the sons die by curse or by sacrifice?**
- Clarke offers another view: Hiel killed his sons as offerings when he laid the foundation and finished the gates. He says the Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) supports this. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/1-kings/16-34.html
- Guzik leaves both options open and quotes Dilday on archaeological evidence of "foundation sacrifices." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-16/
- Smith's commentary reads it as Hiel laying the foundation at Abiram's birth and setting up the gates at Segub's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/16-34.html
- Pulpit's sermon outlines read Jericho as a picture of "Great Babylon" in Revelation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_kings/16.htm

**v. 24, Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says Omri founded Samaria in the sixth year of his reign. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13416a.htm. It also says he moved Israel from hostility toward Judah to friendship. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08193a.htm

**v. 29, Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Ahab's dates in the Bible and in Assyrian records differ, and says the original text of v. 29 may have been changed. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01101b.htm

**v. 31, Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says Jezebel's father was also high priest of Astarte. It says the marriage was likely meant to strengthen Omri's house against Syria, and that Jezebel persuaded Ahab to set up Phoenician worship. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08404a.htm
